lesson_title: How a Cloud Becomes a Star
hook_text: Every star in the sky, including the Sun, started as a cold, dark cloud. Here's how it switches on.
clip_script: Between the stars float huge clouds of hydrogen gas and dust called nebulae. In the thickest parts, gravity starts pulling gas inwards. Sometimes the shock wave from an exploding star gives it a push. As the gas falls in, it squashes, heats up and spins faster, like a skater pulling in her arms, and leftover dust forms a flat disc where planets will grow. The hot ball in the middle is a protostar, a baby star. When its core reaches about 10 million degrees, hydrogen nuclei smash together and fuse into helium, releasing enormous energy. That energy pushes out, gravity pulls in, and when they balance, a star is born. You can see star nurseries like the Orion Nebula from South Africa with just your eyes.
visual_style: A dark nebula slowly collapsing into a spinning glowing disc; a core flashing as fusion ignites; a time-lapse of the Orion Nebula over the Karoo.
pacing: Slow cosmic open, a steady collapse, a dramatic ignition moment, a grounded close under the South African night sky.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find Orion's sword on the next clear night.
